title: The Archive That Could Not Save Everything
passage:
When a small city began digitizing its historical archive, volunteers celebrated the idea of preserving everything forever. The archive contained photographs, letters, meeting records, maps, audio tapes, and thousands of local newspapers. Digital copies seemed safer than fragile paper and old magnetic tape. Yuna, a student volunteer, expected the main challenge to be scanning quickly. Instead, she discovered that preservation required constant choices. Some newspapers could be scanned automatically, but tightly bound books had to be handled page by page. Audio tapes required special equipment and real-time playback. Several photographs had no dates or names, making them difficult to search even after scanning. Storage was another problem. High-quality image files used much more space than compressed copies. Keeping several backup versions reduced the risk of loss but increased cost. The project team had to decide which materials needed the highest quality, which could use smaller files, and which should be processed first. Age alone was not enough to set priorities. A very old printed book might survive safely for decades, while a more recent tape could become unreadable sooner because the playback equipment was disappearing. The archivist described this as a race between physical decay and technological obsolescence. The team also faced questions about access. A family might donate personal letters for historical preservation but not expect them to become searchable online immediately. Some records contained addresses or sensitive details about living people. Making a digital copy did not automatically mean making it public. The archive created separate decisions for preservation and access: an item could be copied for safety while remaining restricted for a period of time. Yuna found this distinction important because she had assumed openness was always the goal of digitization. Volunteers then confronted a less dramatic but equally difficult issue: description. A scanned photograph without useful information might survive perfectly yet remain almost impossible to find. The archive invited older residents to identify buildings, events, and people, but memories sometimes disagreed. Rather than choosing one uncertain answer, staff recorded multiple possibilities and marked them as unconfirmed. This made the catalog less neat but more honest. After six months, only a small portion of the total collection had been digitized. At first, Yuna felt discouraged. The phrase preserve everything had made progress seem like a simple percentage moving toward one hundred. The archivist explained that no archive has unlimited staff, money, storage, or time. Preservation therefore involves deciding what faces the greatest risk, what has high historical value, what communities need, and what future technology may still be able to read. These decisions can later be revised, but delay also has consequences. By the end of her volunteer period, Yuna no longer imagined a digital archive as a perfect copy of the past. It was a carefully maintained bridge between past materials and future users. The bridge needed files, backups, descriptions, privacy rules, equipment, and people who would continue checking whether the system still worked. Digital did not mean permanent. It meant that deterioration changed form: paper could fade, but files could become corrupted, formats could become unsupported, and passwords could be lost. The most important lesson for Yuna was that saving history is not one act of scanning. It is an ongoing practice of selection, documentation, migration, and care under conditions where not everything can be saved at once.

The archive eventually created a priority system with several categories rather than a single ranked list. Materials at immediate risk formed one group, items needed for upcoming community projects formed another, and stable materials of high historical value could wait for slower careful work. The categories were reviewed every few months because risk changed as equipment failed, new donations arrived, or researchers requested access. Staff also tested backups by restoring sample files instead of merely assuming copied files were safe. On one test, an old external drive could not be read by a newer computer without an adapter. The files were still present, but access depended on hardware the team had almost forgotten. This led to an equipment inventory and a schedule for moving files from aging storage. Yuna learned that preservation work is often invisible when it succeeds. Nothing dramatic happens; a file simply opens years later when someone needs it. Those quiet checks protected access just as much as scanning. The team treated successful recovery tests as evidence, not assumptions.
translation:
ある小都市が歴史資料のデジタル化を始めたとき、ボランティアは『すべてを永久に保存できる』と喜びました。写真、手紙、会議記録、地図、音声テープ、新聞などがあり、紙や磁気テープよりデジタルの方が安全に見えました。優奈も大量にスキャンすればよいと思っていましたが、保存には選択の連続が必要だと知ります。新聞は自動処理しやすい一方、製本資料は一ページずつ扱う必要があり、音声テープは専用機器で実時間再生しなければなりません。日付や人物名のない写真はスキャンしても検索しにくいままです。高品質画像は容量が大きく、複数バックアップは安全性を高める一方で費用も増やします。しかも古い物から優先すればよいわけではありません。古い紙の本は何十年も読めても、新しい磁気テープは再生機器が消えて先に読めなくなる可能性があります。担当者はこれを『物理的劣化と技術的陳腐化の競争』と説明しました。公開についても、家族が保存のため寄贈した手紙をすぐネット公開してよいとは限らず、生存者の住所や個人情報を含む資料もあります。そのため『保存するか』と『公開するか』を分け、コピーは安全のため作っても一定期間非公開にする場合があります。また説明情報も重要です。完璧に保存された写真でも何が写っているか分からなければ見つけられません。高齢住民に人物や建物を尋ねても記憶が食い違うことがあり、無理に一つへ決めず複数候補を未確認として記録しました。半年後、デジタル化できたのは全体の一部だけでした。優奈は落胆しましたが、資料館には人員、資金、容量、時間の限界があります。何が失われやすいか、歴史的価値、地域の需要、将来読める技術などを考えて優先順位を決める必要があります。優奈はデジタル資料館を『過去の完全コピー』ではなく、過去の資料と未来の利用者をつなぐ、継続的に維持する橋だと考えるようになりました。紙は色あせ、デジタルはファイル破損、形式の陳腐化、パスワード紛失など別の形で劣化します。歴史を守るとは一度スキャンする行為ではなく、すべてを同時には救えない条件の中で、選択、記録、形式移行、管理を続ける仕事なのです。

資料館は単純な一列の順位ではなく、すぐ劣化する危険がある資料、近い将来の地域企画で必要な資料、安定していて時間をかけて処理できる重要資料など、複数の優先区分を作りました。機器の故障、新しい寄贈、研究者からの利用希望によってリスクは変わるため、数か月ごとに見直しました。また、コピーがあるだけで安全だと思わず、実際にサンプルファイルを復元するテストも行いました。古い外付けドライブが新しいコンピュータではアダプターなしに読めないこともあり、ファイルが存在しても機器がなければ利用できないと分かりました。そこで機器一覧と古い保存媒体からの移行予定を作りました。優奈は、保存が成功しているときほど仕事は目立たず、何年後かに必要なファイルが普通に開くこと自体が成果なのだと理解しました。静かな点検もスキャンと同じくらい大切で、復元できることを実際のテストで確かめるようになりました。
